entities.name: Natural History Museum
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Natural History Museum in London, opened in 1881 in Alfred Waterhouse's Romanesque-Gothic cathedral of science in South Kensington, holds over 80 million specimens — the largest natural history collection in the world — accumulated through 400 years of British imperial scientific expeditions. The museum's collections include specimens gathered by Darwin on the Beagle voyage (1831-1836), type specimens defining over 30,000 species (including the holotype of Homo neanderthalensis), and the most comprehensive collection of meteorites outside the United States.

The museum's origins lie in Hans Sloane's private collection (71,000 objects) purchased by Parliament in 1753 to form the British Museum. Darwin's Beagle specimens, collected 1831-1836, were deposited here — including the Galápagos finches that inspired natural selection theory. The museum's Victorian cathedral-science architecture deliberately echoed medieval cathedrals to position science as humanity's new religion. The central hall's 25-meter diplodocus skeleton (nicknamed Dippy) became the 20th century's most famous museum exhibit.

The NHM's DNA Bank and Frozen Ark program — preserving genetic material from thousands of species — has become critical biodiversity infrastructure as extinction rates accelerate. The museum's citizen science programs engage 400,000 volunteers in monitoring species across Britain. The 2017 replacement of Dippy the diplodocus with a blue whale skeleton (Hope) signaled a deliberate refocus from past wonder to present ecological crisis — one of the most powerful symbolic acts of any museum.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Natural History Museum's 80 million specimens — accumulated through centuries of British scientific expeditions — constitute the world's most comprehensive natural history archive, providing the type specimens and reference collections against which all biological knowledge is measured.
